html:
From 2017 the Chinese government held perhaps a million or more Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other Muslims of Xinjiang in internment camps. Officially they were "vocational education and training centres".

The camps grew out of a "Strike Hard" campaign against terrorism launched in 2014, after violent attacks blamed on Uyghur militants. Under Xi Jinping and the regional party chief Chen Quanguo, who arrived in 2016, people were detained without trial for things like praying, wearing a veil, having relatives abroad or using foreign phone apps. Inside, they had to learn Mandarin and praise the Communist Party. Former detainees have described torture and abuse.

China first denied the camps, then called them schools, and in 2019 said all trainees had graduated. Leaked documents, satellite images and witness accounts told another story. In 2022 the United Nations human rights office said China may have committed crimes against humanity, and several governments call it genocide. The campaign also brought mass surveillance and forced labour, including on cotton farms such as those of the Xinjiang Production Corps.
sum: From 2017 the Chinese government held perhaps a million or more Uyghurs, Kazakhs and other Muslims of Xinjiang in internment camps. Officially they were "vocational education and training centres".
